problem.heading:
What changed around
the collection—and who responds?
problem.intro: Preservation needs more than a room average. Connect the local environment to the collection, building systems and response plan.

cards.title: Cases differ from the gallery
cards.body: Enclosures, shelving and perimeter zones can respond differently to room operation. Pair meaningful reference points before interpreting a change.

cards.title: Water can arrive outside opening hours
cards.body: Leaks near pipework, plant or lower-level stores require a named detection point and a tested callout route.

cards.title: A gap in the environmental record
cards.body: A missing or outdated reading can interrupt a collection review. Check report times against the expected interval and assign retrieval for local loggers so each record has an identifiable observation period.

problem.takeaway: Which collection zone needs investigation, and is the next task for conservation, facilities or the institution’s emergency team?

focus.heading:
Measure the exposure.
Assign the response.
focus.intro: Pair a collection-space reference with the measurements and operating records needed to investigate the actual concern.

stages.title: Define what is vulnerable
stages.body: Identify material groups, case or storage zones, relevant loan conditions and credible water or environmental exposures.

stages.title: Select complementary points
stages.body: Pair room and case climate. Add display-plane light and water-contact points, each with a collection-zone identity and a practical reporting or retrieval plan.

stages.title: Connect the responsible people
stages.body: Conservators assess material implications; facilities staff inspect the relevant building or equipment. Emergency response follows the institution’s plan.

focus.note: Monitoring supports preventive conservation and response. It does not assess an object’s condition or replace dedicated fire, security or emergency systems.
focus.detailTitle: Use measurements appropriate to the collection
focus.detail: Agree criteria for temperature, humidity, duration and change with the conservator. Specify the light sensing plane and any exposure calculation. A lux channel does not measure UV; a general TVOC response does not identify every pollutant of concern to a collection. Select specialist measurements or testing when needed. For water contact, define the sensing coverage and test notifications without exposing collection materials.

applications.heading:
From display cases

cards.title: Galleries & display cases
cards.alt: Museum gallery with enclosed display cases containing collection objects
cards.task: Compare case and gallery climate with display-plane illuminance; include approved case or door-contact events where needed.
cards.placement: Conservation-approved supports, clear of objects; preserve case seals and document the light sensing plane.
cards.response: Collection staff review enclosure or lighting changes with the conservator.

cards.title: Collection stores
cards.alt: Collection storage shelving with archival boxes
cards.task: Combine storage temperature and humidity with point water detection near credible pipework or plant exposures.
cards.placement: Representative shelves and approved floor or plant-adjacent locations, clear of collection objects.
cards.response: Facilities investigates the water source or environmental change; collections staff follow the care or response plan.

cards.title: Paper archives & libraries
cards.alt: Archive storage containing books, paper records and document drawers
cards.task: Follow archive climate, selected air observations, water exposure and access events at rooms with defined risks.
cards.placement: Identified archive zones with representative air exposure; separate doors, vents and perimeter influences.
cards.response: The archive manager reviews material priorities while facilities checks the relevant building conditions.

cards.title: Receiving & acclimatisation rooms
cards.alt: Museum receiving and acclimatisation room with a closed transport crate
cards.task: Compare the receiving-room environment with a retrieved crate-air record where a local logger was specified.
cards.placement: Approved room reference and identified logger position, without contact with the collection itself.
cards.response: The registrar and conservator decide the next handling step under the agreed loan procedure.

faq.q: What is included in Smart Museums & Archives?
faq.a: Begin with temperature, humidity and light at meaningful collection points. Add Hitelecom point water detection near credible leaks. Selected air channels and local loggers address specific investigations; separately chosen door contacts can add opening-state context where needed. The conservation assessment decides the scope, and not every room needs every channel.

faq.q: Should a museum use one temperature and humidity target everywhere?
faq.a: Set criteria with the conservator for the actual material groups, environmental history and loan conditions. Different cases or stores may need different objectives. Use identified records to review the level, duration and change, rather than assuming one room setpoint suits the whole collection.

faq.q: Does air-quality monitoring replace fire detection?
faq.a: No. Particle, TVOC and room-temperature readings support environmental investigation; they do not provide dedicated fire detection. This solution reports sensor data, including direct 4G transmission, and does not include fire-alarm panel integration. The institution retains its separate fire-detection, local warning and emergency arrangements.

faq.q: What does the water-leakage sensor detect?
faq.a: The Hitelecom water-leakage sensor provides point water detection where its compatible probe is installed. It can help identify water near pipework, plant or lower-level stores and start the agreed callout. Coverage depends on the probe position; it does not protect an entire floor automatically. Select a sensing cable or other arrangement separately if wider coverage is required, and test with the actual water conditions.

faq.q: Can door or display-case opening be recorded?
faq.a: Suitable contacts or an authorised access-control interface can supply opening and closing events with a zone identity. Agree whether the task is door-left-open investigation, case handling records or security escalation. These contacts and interfaces are separately selected; environmental monitoring does not replace the institution’s access-control or intrusion-alarm system.

faq.q: Does a lux or TVOC sensor measure every conservation exposure?
faq.a: No. Lux is visible illuminance, not UV. A general TVOC response does not identify every pollutant that may affect collection materials. Agree specialist instruments or tests with the conservator when needed. Accumulated light exposure also requires a defined time-based recording and calculation method.

faq.q: When should we use a local data logger?
faq.a: Use a local recorder for a defined study or journey with planned retrieval, or where a connected installation is unsuitable. H100 stores temperature and humidity for USB readout and PC review. It does not provide live cloud alerts; assign a person and date for retrieval.

faq.q: Can the monitoring records satisfy a lender’s requirements?
faq.a: Confirm the required measurements, accuracy, verification records, timestamps, retention and report format against the actual loan agreement. The system can supply the agreed evidence, with suitable installation and review. Acceptance remains with the institution and lender; monitoring alone does not certify compliance.
